transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-04-08
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Sam Reed (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Jordan Park (Tidewave - Sr Platform Eng), Aisha Romero (Tidewave - SRE Lead), Devon Li (Tidewave - Head of AI Product)

Auto-generated Summary (may be imperfect):
Sam: quick intro, Maya will demo console trace playback and request forensics. Tidewave concerned about intermittent latency spikes and a small set of hallucinations in their QA flows. POC discussion and security checklist.

[00:00:15] Sam Reed (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick round robin? jordan, aisha, devon — do you want to intro your roles briefly?
[00:00:24] Jordan Park (Tidewave): yeah sure, i'm jordan, i run the inference platform at Tidewave. we manage an EKS cluster plus some hosted endpoints for customers. main pain — occasional token stalls and spike latencies at 95th percentile.
[00:00:36] Aisha Romero (Tidewave): hi i'm aisha, lead SRE. we also need auditability for requests-- we have compliance needs and want KMS integration for keys.
[00:00:42] Devon Li (Tidewave): devon here, product. most important for us is stable latency under 200ms p50 for chat completions. also cost matters, but reliability is top.
[00:00:50] Sam: great. maya will take you through a console lab, we'll show trace inspector, request logs, playback and how to map error paths back to prompts and model variants.

[00:01:15] Maya Chen (Redwood SE): ok jumping in, opening the Console. apologies if transcription makes model names weird — the UI section is "Request Inspector". i'll load an example trace. this one is from a synthetic repro we created — request id TW-err-20270401-7.
[00:01:40] Maya: you can see timeline: token generation, KV cache hit/miss annotations, kernel selection note (says quantized-8bit fallback), and then an abrupt latencies spike around step 24.
[00:02:05] Jordan: looks familiar — we've seen that step spike. what's the usual cause? network? kernel fallback?
[00:02:12] Maya: common causes — long prefix leading to larger sequence length, cache eviction, or a fallback to a different model variant due to capacity. Console shows routing decision: our router fell back from rdx-2-8bit to rdx-2-16bit due to memory pressure. that explain the jump.
[00:02:37] Aisha: is that automatic? can we pin to avoid fallback?
[00:02:41] Maya: yes you can pin model versions in the deployment config; for dedicated you can reserve capacity and set a strict routing policy. hosted will do graceful fallback unless you opt out.

[00:03:05] Devon: show us the request logs around that event — i want to see the prompt length distribution.
[00:03:10] Maya: switching to request logs view. okay here's the raw request payload (redacted): user messages, system prompt, attachments. you can filter by token counts, model variant, and observe KV cache hit rate.
[00:03:30] (short pause, typing noises)
[00:03:48] Maya: notice this request had a 2.8k token prefix; KV cache only kept 1.6k because of eviction policy — when the model got a cache miss it had to recompute context which is expensive.
[00:04:05] Jordan: that matches our production logs — long conversations with docs attachments cause evictions. is there a way to pre-warm or pin prefixes?
[00:04:12] Maya: yes — Console suggests prefix caching and also you can use a "sticky cache" option for the KV for sessions. we also have batching controls; Optimize can recommend quantization and batch sizes.

[00:04:40] Maya: now i'll show trace playback — it replays the request and we can step through per-token timing. pressing play...
[00:04:58] [TRACE PLAYBACK] Maya: you can see at ~0:23 the token gen pauses for 1.2s. the timeline shows a kernel selection event and a fallback comment: "insufficient GPU memory, switched kernels".
[00:05:20] Aisha: are those kernel switches visible in logs if we want to ingest into our Splunk?
[00:05:26] Maya: yes, there's an audit log stream you can forward; that's part of the Private plan or Dedicated with advanced observability. Hosted includes a downloadable CSV of request events for 30 days.

[00:05:45] Jordan: about security — we need KMS/HSM integration and full request redaction for PII. how does Redwood handle encryption at rest and auditability?
[00:05:55] Sam: we integrate with customer KMS for Private and Dedicated. for hosted, we provide encrypted keys and can do bring-your-own-key in selected regions. request redaction can be configured on ingestion; we also provide field-level redaction in logs. i'll attach the security deck.
[00:06:20] Devon: do you expose raw requests to your support team?
[00:06:24] Sam: only with a customer explicit consent and it's controlled by RBAC and audit trails.

[00:06:40] Maya: back to the console — here's the error analysis panel. it aggregates error types: timeout, model fallback, low-confidence truncation, tokenization mismatch. you can drill into examples and link them to specific deployment configs and model versions.
[00:07:05] (inaudible)
[00:07:15] Jordan: can you show correlation between request spikes and infra metrics? like GPU memory or host throttling?
[00:07:22] Maya: yep — we surface per-request host metrics, GPU memory consumption, and kernel utilization. there's a correlation chart that overlays request latency with GPU memory usage.
[00:07:40] Aisha: that's useful — when we saw spikes it was right after a nightly ETL that increased prefix sizes.

[00:08:00] Maya: i also want to show the "route history" for a request — which region and pool handled it, and any fallback decisions. this helps when you have multi-region config and want to know why a particular request got routed to a cheaper pool.
[00:08:20] Devon: speaking of cheaper pool — can routing be based on SLOs? e.g., route high-priority customer to dedicated pool?
[00:08:26] Maya: yes, routing policies support rules by customer, token budget, latency SLO and cost tier. you can create a policy to keep premium customers on dedicated nodes.

[00:08:45] Jordan: timeline — we want a POC within two weeks. what would that look like?
[00:08:50] Sam: typical POC: we run a 1-week benchmark against 2 endpoints you pick, measure p50/p95 latency, throughput, and cost. we can run hosted POC or spin up a short-lived dedicated pool. Maya will propose the measurement plan.

[00:09:20] Maya: for the POC i'll need sample traffic patterns and a small set of failing request IDs to validate. i'll also include a script that replays requests at different QPS to simulate your workload.
[00:09:35] Jordan: good. also please include an example of private deployment network diagram — we have strict firewall rules.

[00:09:50] Aisha: compliance questions — do you have SOC 2 type II? ISO? penetration test reports?
[00:09:57] Sam: yes SOC 2 type II available; ISO27001 in progress. i'll include the penetration test summary and our data flow diagram.

[00:10:12] (brief pause)
[00:10:20] Maya: quick demo of the console's debugging runbook: click an example error, there's a suggested troubleshooting checklist — check cache hit ratio, check model variant rollouts, test with pinned model, run a small replay with varying prefix lengths. these are automated suggestions powered by Optimize heuristics.
[00:10:50] Devon: does Optimize actually change configs or just recommend?
[00:10:55] Maya: it recommends; for certain dedicated customers you can enable auto-apply guards but it's opt-in. recommendations include batch size, quantization level, and cache policy tweaks.

[00:11:15] Jordan: latency vs cost — if we pin to avoid fallbacks, what's the typical cost delta?
[00:11:20] Maya: depends on model and QPS. rough ballpark: pinning to dedicated capacity can raise cost 15-40% but reduces p95 variance substantially. Optimize can suggest mixed-policy: pin high-priority traffic and use cheaper pools for low-priority traffic.

[00:11:48] Aisha: what about multi-tenancy isolation in Dedicated? we need workload isolation for compliance.
[00:11:53] Sam: Dedicated gives you isolated GPU pools and network controls. Private (VPC) gives full control over the control plane. RBAC and audit logs are standard.

[00:12:10] (murmurs)
[00:12:18] Maya: i'll now reproduce a KV cache miss scenario with playback. starting replay... you can see token timestamps, and at token 240 the cache miss triggers a recompute.
[00:12:40] Jordan: is it possible to tag session data to persist across requests?
[00:12:44] Maya: yes, sessions can have sticky KV, or you can store context externally and inject a smaller context to avoid eviction. Optimize can detect heavy prefixes and suggest summarization or pinning.

[00:13:10] Devon: gotcha. for PII we can't keep raw user content in logs. can redaction be applied retroactively?
[00:13:18] Maya: we provide field-level redaction at ingestion. retroactive redaction is possible for Private deployments where you control log retention; hosted requires a request but we can purge logs on demand within our retention SLA.

[00:13:40] Jordan: any rate limiting or throttles that could cause spikes? we've seen API throttles cause retries and cascading latency.
[00:13:47] Maya: yes, Console shows rate limit triggers. you can set per-route quotas and token budgets. there's also graceful backpressure and retry policies.

[00:14:10] Aisha: is there telemetry export? we use Datadog and Splunk.
[00:14:14] Maya: yes export integrations for Datadog, Prometheus, and a raw event stream to S3 or Splunk HTTP events.

[00:14:30] (brief silence)
[00:14:40] Sam: quick price note — we'll estimate POC cost after Maya's benchmark plan. dedicated pricing requires a reserved commitment.
[00:14:50] Devon: one last question — model drift / quality regressions: can the console alert on semantic regressions?
[00:14:56] Maya: yes, we have quality monitors that run evals on sample prompts and compare outputs; if similarity or scoring drops we trigger alerts and can tie alerts to rollbacks.

[00:15:20] Jordan: ok that covers the demo. any open technical deep dive we should plan next?
[00:15:25] Aisha: i'd like a dedicated security/deployment scoping call that includes our network and infra teams.
[00:15:30] Sam: we'll set that up. Maya will draft the POC plan and Sam will send security docs.

[00:15:40] (wrap-up)
[00:15:45] Sam: recap: deliver SOC2 + security packet, POC plan, sample replay scripts. tidewave to share failing request IDs and traffic profile. kick off POC week of 4/19.
[00:15:58] Devon: sounds good. thanks both.
[00:16:02] Jordan: thanks, appreciate the quick turn.

[00:16:10] (meeting ends)
